extracted.intended_audience: teachers, students of education, and education theorists
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and standards for organizing curriculum and instruction around experience, activity, and experimental inquiry rather than passive sensation or purely verbal instruction. Emphasizes how schools should select and shape activities so experience becomes meaningful, constructive, and intellectually productive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not reduce judgement and discernment to mere sensations
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject the doctrine that discernment or judgment are 'peculiar sensations' produced solely by the conjoint presence of other sensations; the mind is not merely passive impression-receiver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original discussion: Locke endowed the mind with activities to be exercised upon received material, while some French successors 'razed away the powers and derived them also from impressions received.' Educational implication: preserve and cultivate the mind's active powers (judgment, comparison, abstraction), do not treat them as just another kind of sensory impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Object lessons must not isolate sense-activity as an end
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid making the mere sensory quality or the isolated object-impression the educational end; 'object lessons' that isolate sense-activity tend to become mechanical and to neglect thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: treating instruction as a 'physical gymnastic of the sense-organs' where sensory impressions are sharpened but disconnected from thought. Example critique: excessive isolation of objects magnifies mere physical excitations or heaps up isolated qualities without meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education should be constructive, not merely critical
rubrics_metrics.description: Education's work is constructive—'building up new experience into intellectual habitudes'—rather than simply serving as a dissolvent or critic of existing beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text identifies sensationalism's historical value as critical (dissolving dogmas) but faults it for lacking constructive capacity. Guideline: curricula and methods must aim to form reliable intellectual habits from the start, not just dismantle prior beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete materials as aids to thought but progress to abstractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete objects (beans, counters, pegs) may be helpful as aids to realizing relations, but when employed except as aids to thought they become obstacles to higher understanding; learners must progress from concrete to abstract symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example anti-pattern: prolonging use of physical counters so learning arrests at the level of specific physical symbols. Guidance: design activities so concrete materials support conceptual abstraction; introduce symbols 'whose meaning is realized only through conceptual thinking.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize experience as active and motor, not passive reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience is fundamentally 'a matter of activities, instinctive and impulsive, in their interactions with things'—what is learned are connections discovered through doing, not passive impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical evidence: infants learn by handling, throwing, pounding, etc.; learning concerns what things do in response and what we can do to them. Anti-pattern: schemes that 'ignore and as far as may be exclude the natural tendency to learn about the qualities of objects by the uses to which they are put.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform experience into deliberate experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience should be experimental—deliberate control of activity with aims and methods so that what happens becomes 'fertile of suggestions' and a means for testing hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare scientific experimental method: alter and extend sense-data (telescope, microscope), act on objects under controlled conditions to arouse hypotheses. Guideline: school experiences should be planned, measured, and methodical rather than chance occurrences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectualize practical pursuits—integrate doing and knowing
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical activities in school should be selected and organized to 'intellectualize' them—making doing a vehicle for understanding rather than routine skill for external ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schools should not transport youth from active environments into cramped study detached from action, but should move them from chance activities to activities selected 'with reference to guidance of learning.' Practical pursuits must be used to cultivate comprehension, initiative, and inventiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt the laboratory/discovery method broadly and early
rubrics_metrics.description: The laboratory method—experimentation under conditions of deliberate control—should be a central and early resource in education, not an isolated tool used only when pupils are older.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem: laboratories too often 'remain too largely but an isolated resource' and are not integrated with other studies, reducing their educational benefit. Guideline: integrate experimental inquiry across subjects so laboratory work contributes to intellectual development, not only technical skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance naturalistic (scientific) and humanistic studies; serve human ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Naturalistic studies are indispensable but should be pursued in service of humanistic and moral ends; science and humanities should be connected rather than pitted as rivals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical perspective: Plato and Aristotle subordinated or used natural studies to illuminate human ends. Educational implication: curriculum design should reflect the unity of nature and human affairs, using scientific knowledge to support the 'supreme purpose of existence' and human values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reducing science education to mechanical, quantitative technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not mistake scientific technique, apparatus, and terminology for the whole of scientific subject matter; education should preserve qualitative human values and meanings, not only quantitative control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique: mechanical philosophy treats objective existence as only quantitative (mass and motion) and ignores qualitative distinctions (colors, sounds, goods, ends). Guideline: science teaching must not strip phenomena of their qualitative significance or present science as only prediction and control.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-hand acquaintance is essential but limited in scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Empiricism's insistence on 'first-hand element'—impression made upon me—is valuable, but direct impression is limited in range and cannot be the sole basis of broad knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text warning: 'the further we get away from this direct, first-hand source of knowledge, the more numerous the sources of error' yet relying only on direct acquaintance 'is fatally restricted' for subjects (e.g., geography beyond immediate surroundings). Use first-hand experiences as a foundation but supplement them to extend range and meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associate linguistic symbols with prior presentations of objects for meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Words and linguistic symbols, without prior presentations of objects to associate with them, convey nothing but 'sensations of their own shape and color' and do not yield instructive knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline for instruction: ensure verbal-symbolic instruction is grounded in concrete experiences or representations so that language stands for meanings, not merely for isolated sounds or shapes.
